questions.question_html: Let $a,b \in ℂ$ . Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ . If $\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$ and $\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=3i\sqrt{11}$ , then $(\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3})^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Given: $\alpha,\beta$ are roots of $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ $\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$ $\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=3i\sqrt{11}$ We have to find $(\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3})^{2}$ . Now, $\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta+\alpha)$ Substituting the given values, $3i\sqrt{11}=\sqrt{11}(\beta+\alpha)$ Since $\sqrt{11} \ne 0$ , we get $\beta+\alpha=3i$ Now use the identity $\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2})$ So first let us find $\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2}$ . We know $(\beta+\alpha)^{2}=\beta^{2}+\alpha^{2}+2\alpha\beta$ Also, $\alpha\beta=\frac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-(\beta-\alpha)^{2}}{4}$ Substitute the values: $\alpha+\beta=3i,\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$ Thus, $\alpha\beta=\frac{(3i)^{2}-(\sqrt{11})^{2}}{4}=\frac{-9-11}{4}=\frac{-20}{4}=-5$ Now, $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-2\alpha\beta$ So, $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(3i)^{2}-2(-5)=-9+10=1$ Hence, $\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2}=1+(-5)=-4$ Therefore, $\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2})=\sqrt{11} \cdot (-4)=-4\sqrt{11}$ Now square it: $(\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3})^{2}=(-4\sqrt{11})^{2}=16 \cdot 11=176$ So the correct answer is: $176$ Hence, Option B is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

  • $\alpha,\beta$ are roots of $x^{2}+ax+b=0$

  • $\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$

  • $\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=3i\sqrt{11}$

We have to find $(\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3})^{2}$ .

Now,

$\beta^{2}-\alpha^{2}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta+\alpha)$

Substituting the given values,

$3i\sqrt{11}=\sqrt{11}(\beta+\alpha)$

Since $\sqrt{11} \ne 0$ , we get

$\beta+\alpha=3i$

Now use the identity

$\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2})$

So first let us find $\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2}$ .

We know

$(\beta+\alpha)^{2}=\beta^{2}+\alpha^{2}+2\alpha\beta$

Also,

$\alpha\beta=\frac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-(\beta-\alpha)^{2}}{4}$

Substitute the values:

$\alpha+\beta=3i,\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$

Thus,

$\alpha\beta=\frac{(3i)^{2}-(\sqrt{11})^{2}}{4}=\frac{-9-11}{4}=\frac{-20}{4}=-5$

Now,

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-2\alpha\beta$

So,

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(3i)^{2}-2(-5)=-9+10=1$

Hence,

$\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2}=1+(-5)=-4$

Therefore,

$\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3}=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta+\alpha^{2})=\sqrt{11} \cdot (-4)=-4\sqrt{11}$

Now square it:

$(\beta^{3}-\alpha^{3})^{2}=(-4\sqrt{11})^{2}=16 \cdot 11=176$

So the correct answer is:

$176$

Hence, Option B is correct.

questions.question_html: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $50(\frac{2x}{1+3i}-\frac{y}{1-2i})=31+17i,i=\sqrt{-1}$ . Then the value of $10(x-3y)$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $50(\frac{2x}{1+3i}-\frac{y}{1-2i})=31+17i$ We need to find $10(x-3y)$ . First, simplify the fractions by rationalising the denominators. $\frac{2x}{1+3i}=\frac{2x(1-3i)}{(1+3i)(1-3i)}$ $=\frac{2x(1-3i)}{1+9}=\frac{2x(1-3i)}{10}$ $=\frac{x}{5}(1-3i)$ Similarly, $\frac{y}{1-2i}=\frac{y(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}$ $=\frac{y(1+2i)}{1+4}=\frac{y(1+2i)}{5}$ Now substitute into the given equation: $50(\frac{x}{5}(1-3i)-\frac{y}{5}(1+2i))=31+17i$ Take $\frac{1}{5}$ common inside: $50 \cdot \frac{1}{5}[x(1-3i)-y(1+2i)]=31+17i$ $10[x(1-3i)-y(1+2i)]=31+17i$ Expand: $10[x-3xi-y-2yi]=31+17i$ $10[(x-y)+(-3x-2y)i]=31+17i$ So, $10(x-y)+10(-3x-2y)i=31+17i$ Now compare real and imaginary parts: $10(x-y)=31$ $10(-3x-2y)=17$ Thus, $x-y=\frac{31}{10}$ $-3x-2y=\frac{17}{10}$ Now solve these equations. From the first equation, $x=y+\frac{31}{10}$ Substitute into the second: $-3(y+\frac{31}{10})-2y=\frac{17}{10}$ $-3y-\frac{93}{10}-2y=\frac{17}{10}$ $-5y=\frac{17}{10}+\frac{93}{10}$ $-5y=\frac{110}{10}=11$ $y=-\frac{11}{5}$ Then $x=y+\frac{31}{10}=-\frac{11}{5}+\frac{31}{10}$ $x=-\frac{22}{10}+\frac{31}{10}=\frac{9}{10}$ Now find: $10(x-3y)=10(\frac{9}{10}-3(-\frac{11}{5}))$ $=10(\frac{9}{10}+\frac{33}{5})$ $=10(\frac{9}{10}+\frac{66}{10})$ $=10 \cdot \frac{75}{10}=75$ Therefore, the value of $10(x-3y)$ is $75$ So, the correct option is $\text{D}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
$50(\frac{2x}{1+3i}-\frac{y}{1-2i})=31+17i$

We need to find $10(x-3y)$ .

First, simplify the fractions by rationalising the denominators.

$\frac{2x}{1+3i}=\frac{2x(1-3i)}{(1+3i)(1-3i)}$

$=\frac{2x(1-3i)}{1+9}=\frac{2x(1-3i)}{10}$

$=\frac{x}{5}(1-3i)$

Similarly,

$\frac{y}{1-2i}=\frac{y(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}$

$=\frac{y(1+2i)}{1+4}=\frac{y(1+2i)}{5}$

Now substitute into the given equation:

$50(\frac{x}{5}(1-3i)-\frac{y}{5}(1+2i))=31+17i$

Take $\frac{1}{5}$ common inside:

$50 \cdot \frac{1}{5}[x(1-3i)-y(1+2i)]=31+17i$

$10[x(1-3i)-y(1+2i)]=31+17i$

Expand:

$10[x-3xi-y-2yi]=31+17i$

$10[(x-y)+(-3x-2y)i]=31+17i$

So,

$10(x-y)+10(-3x-2y)i=31+17i$

Now compare real and imaginary parts:

$10(x-y)=31$

$10(-3x-2y)=17$

Thus,

$x-y=\frac{31}{10}$

$-3x-2y=\frac{17}{10}$

Now solve these equations.

From the first equation,

$x=y+\frac{31}{10}$

Substitute into the second:

$-3(y+\frac{31}{10})-2y=\frac{17}{10}$

$-3y-\frac{93}{10}-2y=\frac{17}{10}$

$-5y=\frac{17}{10}+\frac{93}{10}$

$-5y=\frac{110}{10}=11$

$y=-\frac{11}{5}$

Then

$x=y+\frac{31}{10}=-\frac{11}{5}+\frac{31}{10}$

$x=-\frac{22}{10}+\frac{31}{10}=\frac{9}{10}$

Now find:

$10(x-3y)=10(\frac{9}{10}-3(-\frac{11}{5}))$

$=10(\frac{9}{10}+\frac{33}{5})$

$=10(\frac{9}{10}+\frac{66}{10})$

$=10 \cdot \frac{75}{10}=75$

Therefore, the value of $10(x-3y)$ is

$75$

So, the correct option is $\text{D}$ .

questions.question_html: If $z=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{i}{2},i=\sqrt{-1}$ , then $(z^{201}-i)^{8}$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: $z=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{i}{2}$ Convert into Euler form $z=re^{i\theta}$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta=arg(z)=tan^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})$ if $z=x+iy$ . $r=|z|=\sqrt{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})^{2}+(\frac{1}{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}}=1$ Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant in the complex plane, $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\theta=tan^{-1}(\frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2})=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & z=e^{i\frac{\pi}{6}} \end{aligned}$ To calculate $(z^{201}-i)^{8}=((e^{i\frac{\pi}{6}})^{201}-i)^{8}$ $=(e^{i\frac{201\pi}{6}}-i)^{8}$ Using De Moivre's theorem, $e^{i\theta}=cos\theta+isin\theta$ $\begin{aligned} & (z^{201}-i)^{8}=(cos(\frac{201\pi}{6})+isin(\frac{201\pi}{6})-i)^{8} \\ & =(cos(\frac{67\pi}{2})+isin(\frac{67\pi}{2})-i)^{8} \\ & =(0+i(-1)-i)^{8} \\ & =(-2i)^{8}=2^{8}(i)^{8} \end{aligned}$ Since $i=\sqrt{-1}⟹i^{2}=-1⟹i^{4}=1⟹i^{8}=1$ $\therefore$ $(z^{201}-i)^{8}=2^{8}=256$ .

$r=|z|=\sqrt{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})^{2}+(\frac{1}{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}}=1$

Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant in the complex plane,

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}\theta=tan^{-1}(\frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2})=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & z=e^{i\frac{\pi}{6}} \end{aligned}$

To calculate $(z^{201}-i)^{8}=((e^{i\frac{\pi}{6}})^{201}-i)^{8}$

$=(e^{i\frac{201\pi}{6}}-i)^{8}$

Using De Moivre's theorem, $e^{i\theta}=cos\theta+isin\theta$

$\begin{aligned} & (z^{201}-i)^{8}=(cos(\frac{201\pi}{6})+isin(\frac{201\pi}{6})-i)^{8} \\ & =(cos(\frac{67\pi}{2})+isin(\frac{67\pi}{2})-i)^{8} \\ & =(0+i(-1)-i)^{8} \\ & =(-2i)^{8}=2^{8}(i)^{8} \end{aligned}$

Since $i=\sqrt{-1}⟹i^{2}=-1⟹i^{4}=1⟹i^{8}=1$

$\therefore$ $(z^{201}-i)^{8}=2^{8}=256$ .

By the definition of an ellipse, the sum of distances from two fixed points (foci) is constant. Here, the foci are $F_{1}(2,0)$ and $F_{2}(-2,0)$ , and the length of the major axis $2a=5$ , so $a=2.5$ . By the definition of an ellipse, the sum of distances from two fixed points (foci) is constant. Here, the foci are $F_{1}(2,0)$ and $F_{2}(-2,0)$ , and the length of the major axis $2a=5$ , so $a=2.5$ . The distance between foci is $2ae=4$ , so $e=\frac{4}{5}=0.8$ . The semi-minor axis $b$ can be found using $b^{2}=a^{2}(1-e^{2})=(2.5)^{2}(1-0.64)=6.25(0.36)=2.25$ , so $b=1.5$ . The ellipse is centered at the origin $(0,0)$ and extends from $x=-2.5$ to $x=2.5$ along the real axis. To find $max{|z_{1}-z_{2}|:z_{1} \in A$ and $z_{2} \in B}$ This means maximize the distance between a point $z_{1}$ in the circle and a point $z_{2}$ on the ellipse. The furthest point in set $A$ (the circle) is at the rightmost edge, $z_{1}=(2+4,0)=(6,0)$ . The furthest point in set $B$ (the ellipse) from $z_{1}$ is at its leftmost edge, $z_{2}=(-2.5,0)$ . Maximum Distance $|z_{1}-z_{2}|=|6-(-2.5)|=|6+2.5|=8.5=\frac{17}{2}$

questions.explanation_text: Let $z=x+iy\text{where}x,y \in ℝ.$ Then $\bar{z}=x-iy.$ The given equation is $z(\bar{z}+2+i)+k(2+3i)=0.$ We have to find all real values of $k$ for which this equation has at least one complex solution $z$ . First, simplify $z(\bar{z}+2+i)$ : $z(\bar{z}+2+i)=z\bar{z}+z(2+i).$ Now, $z\bar{z}=|z|^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$ and $z(2+i)=(x+iy)(2+i).$ Let us multiply: $(x+iy)(2+i)=2x+ix+2iy+i^{2}y$ Since $i^{2}=-1$ , $(x+iy)(2+i)=(2x-y)+i(x+2y).$ So, $z(\bar{z}+2+i)=x^{2}+y^{2}+(2x-y)+i(x+2y).$ Hence the given equation becomes $(x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y)+i(x+2y)+k(2+3i)=0.$ Now separate real and imaginary parts: $(x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y+2k)+i(x+2y+3k)=0.$ Therefore, $x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y+2k=0\text{and}x+2y+3k=0.$ From the second equation, $3k=-(x+2y)$ so $k=-\frac{x+2y}{3}.$ Substitute this into the first equation: $x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y+2(-\frac{x+2y}{3})=0.$ Multiply by $3$ : $3x^{2}+3y^{2}+6x-3y-2x-4y=0$ $3x^{2}+3y^{2}+4x-7y=0.$ Now complete squares: $3(x^{2}+\frac{4}{3}x)+3(y^{2}-\frac{7}{3}y)=0.$ $3[(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}-\frac{4}{9}]+3[(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}-\frac{49}{36}]=0.$ $3(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}-\frac{4}{3}+3(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}-\frac{49}{12}=0.$ $3(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}+3(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{49}{12}.$ $3(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}+3(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}=\frac{16+49}{12}=\frac{65}{12}.$ So, $(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}+(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}=\frac{65}{36}.$ This is a circle with centre $(-\frac{2}{3},\frac{7}{6})$ and radius $\frac{\sqrt{65}}{6}.$ Now, $k=-\frac{x+2y}{3}.$ So we need the range of the linear expression $x+2y$ on this circle. Let $S=x+2y.$ For a circle, maximum and minimum of a linear expression occur at the extreme points in the direction of its normal vector. At the centre, $S_{c}=-\frac{2}{3}+2 \cdot \frac{7}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{7}{3}=\frac{5}{3}.$ The vector corresponding to $x+2y$ is $(1,2)$ , whose magnitude is $\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{5}.$ Hence the maximum variation from the centre is $\text{radius} \times \sqrt{5}=\frac{\sqrt{65}}{6} \cdot \sqrt{5}=\frac{\sqrt{325}}{6}=\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}.$ Therefore, $S_{min}=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6},S_{max}=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}.$ Since $k=-\frac{S}{3},$ the interval for $k$ is $[-\frac{S_{max}}{3},-\frac{S_{min}}{3}].$ So if this interval is $[\alpha,\beta]$ , then $\alpha+\beta=-\frac{S_{max}+S_{min}}{3}=-\frac{2 \cdot \frac{5}{3}}{3}=-\frac{10}{9}.$ Hence, $9(\alpha+\beta)=9(-\frac{10}{9})=-10.$ Therefore, the correct answer is $-10.$ So, Option A is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$z=x+iy\text{where}x,y \in ℝ.$

Then

$\bar{z}=x-iy.$

The given equation is

$z(\bar{z}+2+i)+k(2+3i)=0.$

We have to find all real values of $k$ for which this equation has at least one complex solution $z$ .

First, simplify $z(\bar{z}+2+i)$ :

$z(\bar{z}+2+i)=z\bar{z}+z(2+i).$

Now,

$z\bar{z}=|z|^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$

and

$z(2+i)=(x+iy)(2+i).$

Let us multiply:

$(x+iy)(2+i)=2x+ix+2iy+i^{2}y$

Since $i^{2}=-1$ ,

$(x+iy)(2+i)=(2x-y)+i(x+2y).$

So,

$z(\bar{z}+2+i)=x^{2}+y^{2}+(2x-y)+i(x+2y).$

Hence the given equation becomes

$(x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y)+i(x+2y)+k(2+3i)=0.$

Now separate real and imaginary parts:

$(x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y+2k)+i(x+2y+3k)=0.$

Therefore,

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y+2k=0\text{and}x+2y+3k=0.$

From the second equation,

$3k=-(x+2y)$

so

$k=-\frac{x+2y}{3}.$

Substitute this into the first equation:

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-y+2(-\frac{x+2y}{3})=0.$

Multiply by $3$ :

$3x^{2}+3y^{2}+6x-3y-2x-4y=0$

$3x^{2}+3y^{2}+4x-7y=0.$

Now complete squares:

$3(x^{2}+\frac{4}{3}x)+3(y^{2}-\frac{7}{3}y)=0.$

$3[(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}-\frac{4}{9}]+3[(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}-\frac{49}{36}]=0.$

$3(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}-\frac{4}{3}+3(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}-\frac{49}{12}=0.$

$3(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}+3(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{49}{12}.$

$3(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}+3(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}=\frac{16+49}{12}=\frac{65}{12}.$

So,

$(x+\frac{2}{3})^{2}+(y-\frac{7}{6})^{2}=\frac{65}{36}.$

This is a circle with centre

$(-\frac{2}{3},\frac{7}{6})$

and radius

$\frac{\sqrt{65}}{6}.$

Now,

$k=-\frac{x+2y}{3}.$

So we need the range of the linear expression $x+2y$ on this circle.

Let

$S=x+2y.$

For a circle, maximum and minimum of a linear expression occur at the extreme points in the direction of its normal vector.

At the centre,

$S_{c}=-\frac{2}{3}+2 \cdot \frac{7}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{7}{3}=\frac{5}{3}.$

The vector corresponding to $x+2y$ is $(1,2)$ , whose magnitude is

$\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{5}.$

Hence the maximum variation from the centre is

$\text{radius} \times \sqrt{5}=\frac{\sqrt{65}}{6} \cdot \sqrt{5}=\frac{\sqrt{325}}{6}=\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}.$

Therefore,

$S_{min}=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6},S_{max}=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{5\sqrt{13}}{6}.$

Since

$k=-\frac{S}{3},$

the interval for $k$ is

$[-\frac{S_{max}}{3},-\frac{S_{min}}{3}].$

So if this interval is $[\alpha,\beta]$ , then

$\alpha+\beta=-\frac{S_{max}+S_{min}}{3}=-\frac{2 \cdot \frac{5}{3}}{3}=-\frac{10}{9}.$

Hence,

$9(\alpha+\beta)=9(-\frac{10}{9})=-10.$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$-10.$

So, Option A is correct.

questions.question_html: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $|z+2|=|z-2|$ and arg $(\frac{z+3}{z-i})=\frac{\pi}{4}$ . Then $|z|^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Let $z=x+iy$ where $x,y \in ℝ$ . We are given: $|z+2|=|z-2|$ and $arg(\frac{z+3}{z-i})=\frac{\pi}{4}$ We will use these one by one. 1. Using $|z+2|=|z-2|$ Substitute $z=x+iy$ : $|x+iy+2|=|x+iy-2|$ So, $\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}+y^{2}}=\sqrt{(x-2)^{2}+y^{2}}$ Squaring both sides: $(x+2)^{2}+y^{2}=(x-2)^{2}+y^{2}$ $x^{2}+4x+4=x^{2}-4x+4$ $8x=0$ $x=0$ Hence, $z=iy$ So the point lies on the imaginary axis. 2. Using the argument condition Now, $\frac{z+3}{z-i}=\frac{3+iy}{i(y-1)}$ We are given that its argument is $\frac{\pi}{4}$ . A complex number has argument $\frac{\pi}{4}$ when its real and imaginary parts are equal and positive in sign together. Let us simplify: $\frac{3+iy}{i(y-1)}$ Since $\frac{1}{i}=-i$ , we get $\frac{3+iy}{i(y-1)}=\frac{-i(3+iy)}{y-1}$ Now expand: $-i(3+iy)=-3i-i^{2}y=y-3i$ So, $\frac{z+3}{z-i}=\frac{y-3i}{y-1}=\frac{y}{y-1}-i\frac{3}{y-1}$ Thus real part is $\frac{y}{y-1}$ and imaginary part is $-\frac{3}{y-1}$ Since argument is $\frac{\pi}{4}$ , we need $\frac{\text{imaginary part}}{\text{real part}}=tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$ So, $\frac{-\frac{3}{y-1}}{\frac{y}{y-1}}=1$ $-\frac{3}{y}=1$ $y=-3$ Therefore, $z=-3i$ 3. Find $|z|^{2}$ $|z|^{2}=0^{2}+(-3)^{2}=9$ So, $9$ Hence, the correct option is Option A .
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$z=x+iy$

where $x,y \in ℝ$ .

We are given:

$|z+2|=|z-2|$

and

$arg(\frac{z+3}{z-i})=\frac{\pi}{4}$

We will use these one by one.

1. Using $|z+2|=|z-2|$

Substitute $z=x+iy$ :

$|x+iy+2|=|x+iy-2|$

So,

$\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}+y^{2}}=\sqrt{(x-2)^{2}+y^{2}}$

Squaring both sides:

$(x+2)^{2}+y^{2}=(x-2)^{2}+y^{2}$

$x^{2}+4x+4=x^{2}-4x+4$

$8x=0$

$x=0$

Hence,

$z=iy$

So the point lies on the imaginary axis.

2. Using the argument condition

Now,

$\frac{z+3}{z-i}=\frac{3+iy}{i(y-1)}$

We are given that its argument is $\frac{\pi}{4}$ .

A complex number has argument $\frac{\pi}{4}$ when its real and imaginary parts are equal and positive in sign together.

Let us simplify:

$\frac{3+iy}{i(y-1)}$

Since $\frac{1}{i}=-i$ , we get

$\frac{3+iy}{i(y-1)}=\frac{-i(3+iy)}{y-1}$

Now expand:

$-i(3+iy)=-3i-i^{2}y=y-3i$

So,

$\frac{z+3}{z-i}=\frac{y-3i}{y-1}=\frac{y}{y-1}-i\frac{3}{y-1}$

Thus real part is

$\frac{y}{y-1}$

and imaginary part is

$-\frac{3}{y-1}$

Since argument is $\frac{\pi}{4}$ , we need

$\frac{\text{imaginary part}}{\text{real part}}=tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$

So,

$\frac{-\frac{3}{y-1}}{\frac{y}{y-1}}=1$

$-\frac{3}{y}=1$

$y=-3$

Therefore,

$z=-3i$

3. Find $|z|^{2}$

$|z|^{2}=0^{2}+(-3)^{2}=9$

So,

$9$

Hence, the correct option is Option A.

questions.question_html: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $|z-6|=5$ and $|z+2-6i|=5$ . Then the value of $z^{3}+3z^{2}-15z+141$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let $z=x+iy$ $|z-(\alpha+i\beta)|=r$ represents a circle in the complex plane with centre at $(\alpha,\beta)$ and radius is $r$ unit. Cartesian equation $(x-\alpha)^{2}+(y-\beta)^{2}=r^{2}$ The equations $|z-6|=5$ and $|z-(-2+6i)|=5$ describe two circles with the same radius $(r=5)$ . Circle 1 : Center $C_{1}=(6,0)$ Circle 2 : Center $C_{2}=(-2,6)$ Cartesian equation $(x-6)^{2}+y^{2}=25\text{and}(x+2)^{2}+(y-6)^{2}=25$ Expanding both: $x^{2}-12x+36+y^{2}=25⟹x^{2}+y^{2}-12x+𝟏𝟏=𝟎...(i)$ $x^{2}+4x+4+y^{2}-12y+36=25⟹x^{2}+y^{2}+𝟒x-𝟏𝟐y+𝟏𝟓=𝟎...(ii)$ Subtracting the first equation from the second to find the common chord: $\begin{aligned} (4x-(-12x))-12y+(15-11)=0 \\ 16x-12y+4=0⟹𝟒-𝟑y+𝟏=𝟎⟹y=\frac{𝟒x+𝟏}{𝟑} \end{aligned}$ Substitute $y$ back into the first circle equation: $(x-6)^{2}+(\frac{4x+1}{3})^{2}=25$ multiply both sides by 9 $\begin{aligned} & 9(x^{2}+36-12x)+16x^{2}+8x+1=225 \\ & 25x^{2}-100x+100=0 \\ & x^{2}-4x+4=0 \\ & (x-2)^{2}=0 \Rightarrow x=2 \end{aligned}$ put $x=2$ in $y=(4x+1)/3$ $y=(4 \times 2+1)/3=9/3=3$ $\text{so}z=2+3i$ calculate $z^{3}+3z^{2}-15z+141$ Compute $z^{3}$ $\begin{aligned} z^{3}=z \cdot z^{2}=(2+3i)(-5+12i) \\ =-10+24i-15i+36i^{2} \\ =-10+9i-36 \\ =-46+9i \end{aligned}$ Compute $z^{2}$ $(2+3i)^{2}=4+12i+9i^{2}=4+12i-9=-5+12i$ so $\begin{aligned} z^{3}=-46+9i \\ 3z^{2}=-15+36i \\ -15z=-30-45i \end{aligned}$ Add everything $(-46+9i)+(-15+36i)+(-30-45i)+141$ Real parts: $-46-15-30+141=50$ Imaginary parts: $9i+36i-45i=0$ So $z^{3}+3z^{2}-15z+141=50$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $z=x+iy$

$|z-(\alpha+i\beta)|=r$ represents a circle in the complex plane with centre at $(\alpha,\beta)$ and radius is $r$ unit.

Cartesian equation

$(x-\alpha)^{2}+(y-\beta)^{2}=r^{2}$

The equations $|z-6|=5$ and $|z-(-2+6i)|=5$ describe two circles with the same radius $(r=5)$ .

  • Circle 1 : Center $C_{1}=(6,0)$

  • Circle 2 : Center $C_{2}=(-2,6)$

Cartesian equation

$(x-6)^{2}+y^{2}=25\text{and}(x+2)^{2}+(y-6)^{2}=25$

Expanding both:

  • $x^{2}-12x+36+y^{2}=25⟹x^{2}+y^{2}-12x+𝟏𝟏=𝟎...(i)$

  • $x^{2}+4x+4+y^{2}-12y+36=25⟹x^{2}+y^{2}+𝟒x-𝟏𝟐y+𝟏𝟓=𝟎...(ii)$

Subtracting the first equation from the second to find the common chord:

$\begin{aligned} (4x-(-12x))-12y+(15-11)=0 \\ 16x-12y+4=0⟹𝟒-𝟑y+𝟏=𝟎⟹y=\frac{𝟒x+𝟏}{𝟑} \end{aligned}$

Substitute $y$ back into the first circle equation:

$(x-6)^{2}+(\frac{4x+1}{3})^{2}=25$

multiply both sides by 9

$\begin{aligned} & 9(x^{2}+36-12x)+16x^{2}+8x+1=225 \\ & 25x^{2}-100x+100=0 \\ & x^{2}-4x+4=0 \\ & (x-2)^{2}=0 \Rightarrow x=2 \end{aligned}$

put $x=2$ in $y=(4x+1)/3$

$y=(4 \times 2+1)/3=9/3=3$

$\text{so}z=2+3i$

calculate $z^{3}+3z^{2}-15z+141$

Compute $z^{3}$

$\begin{aligned} z^{3}=z \cdot z^{2}=(2+3i)(-5+12i) \\ =-10+24i-15i+36i^{2} \\ =-10+9i-36 \\ =-46+9i \end{aligned}$

Compute $z^{2}$

$(2+3i)^{2}=4+12i+9i^{2}=4+12i-9=-5+12i$

so

$\begin{aligned} z^{3}=-46+9i \\ 3z^{2}=-15+36i \\ -15z=-30-45i \end{aligned}$

Add everything

$(-46+9i)+(-15+36i)+(-30-45i)+141$

Real parts:

$-46-15-30+141=50$

Imaginary parts:

$9i+36i-45i=0$

So $z^{3}+3z^{2}-15z+141=50$

questions.question_html:
Let $z_{1},z_{2} \in ℂ$ be the distinct solutions of the equation $z^{2}+4z-(1+12i)=0$ .

Then $|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given the quadratic equation $z^{2}+4z-(1+12i)=0$ let its roots be $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ . We need to find $|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}$ Using Vieta’s formulas for $az^{2}+bz+c=0,$ we have $z_{1}+z_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}=-4$ and $z_{1}z_{2}=\frac{c}{a}=-(1+12i)=-1-12i$ Now solve the equation to identify the roots. $z^{2}+4z-(1+12i)=0$ Using the quadratic formula, $z=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16+4(1+12i)}}{2}$ $z=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{20+48i}}{2}$ Now observe that $(6+4i)^{2}=36+48i-16=20+48i$ So, $\sqrt{20+48i}=6+4i$ Hence the roots are $z_{1}=\frac{-4+(6+4i)}{2}=1+2i$ and $z_{2}=\frac{-4-(6+4i)}{2}=-5-2i$ Now compute their moduli squared: $|z_{1}|^{2}=|1+2i|^{2}=1^{2}+2^{2}=5$ $|z_{2}|^{2}=|-5-2i|^{2}=(-5)^{2}+(-2)^{2}=25+4=29$ Therefore, $|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}=5+29=34$ So the correct answer is $34$ Hence, Option D is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Given the quadratic equation

$z^{2}+4z-(1+12i)=0$

let its roots be $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ .

We need to find

$|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}$

Using Vieta’s formulas for

$az^{2}+bz+c=0,$

we have

$z_{1}+z_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}=-4$

and

$z_{1}z_{2}=\frac{c}{a}=-(1+12i)=-1-12i$

Now solve the equation to identify the roots.

$z^{2}+4z-(1+12i)=0$

Using the quadratic formula,

$z=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16+4(1+12i)}}{2}$

$z=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{20+48i}}{2}$

Now observe that

$(6+4i)^{2}=36+48i-16=20+48i$

So,

$\sqrt{20+48i}=6+4i$

Hence the roots are

$z_{1}=\frac{-4+(6+4i)}{2}=1+2i$

and

$z_{2}=\frac{-4-(6+4i)}{2}=-5-2i$

Now compute their moduli squared:

$|z_{1}|^{2}=|1+2i|^{2}=1^{2}+2^{2}=5$

$|z_{2}|^{2}=|-5-2i|^{2}=(-5)^{2}+(-2)^{2}=25+4=29$

Therefore,

$|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}=5+29=34$

So the correct answer is

$34$

Hence, Option D is correct.

Let the circles $C_{1}:|z|=r$ and $C_{2}:|z-3-4i|=5$ , $z \in ℂ$ , be such that $C_{2}$ lies within $C_{1}$ .
If $z_{1}$ moves on $C_{1}$ , $z_{2}$ moves on $C_{2}$ and $min|z_{1}-z_{2}|=2$ , then $max|z_{1}-z_{2}|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & |z|=r \\ & OA=r \end{aligned}$ Step 1: Circle $C_{1}:|z|=r$ has centre $O(0,0)$ and radius $r$ (so $OA=r$ ). Their arguments are as follows: $arg(z_{1})=-\frac{\pi}{4}$ $arg(z_{2})=0$ $arg(z_{3})=\frac{\pi}{4}$ Thus, the complex numbers can be represented as: $z_{1}=e^{-i\frac{\pi}{4}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$ $z_{2}=e^{i \cdot 0}=1$ $z_{3}=e^{i\frac{\pi}{4}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$ Next, calculate the conjugates needed: $\bar{z}_{2}=1$ $\bar{z}_{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\bar{z}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$ We need to evaluate: $z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}+z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}+z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}$ Calculate each term separately: $z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}) \cdot 1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$ $z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}=1 \cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$ $z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}) \cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{(1+i)^{2}}{2}=\frac{1+2i-1}{2}=i$ Sum the evaluated terms: $z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}+z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}+z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})+i$ Simplify: $=\sqrt{2}+i-\sqrt{2}i=\sqrt{2}+i(1-\sqrt{2})$ Calculate the modulus squared: $|\sqrt{2}+i(1-\sqrt{2})|^{2}=(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(1-\sqrt{2})^{2}$ $=2+(1-2\sqrt{2}+2)=5-2\sqrt{2}$ Thus, the expression $|z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}+z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}+z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}|^{2}$ simplifies as follows: $\alpha=5$ $\beta=-2$ Finally, compute $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ : $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=5^{2}+(-2)^{2}=25+4=29$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is 29.
questions.explanation_html:
To solve the problem, we start with the given information about the complex numbers $z_{1},z_{2},$ and $z_{3}$ , which lie on the unit circle $|z|=1$ . Their arguments are as follows:

$arg(z_{1})=-\frac{\pi}{4}$

$arg(z_{2})=0$

$arg(z_{3})=\frac{\pi}{4}$

Thus, the complex numbers can be represented as:

$z_{1}=e^{-i\frac{\pi}{4}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$

$z_{2}=e^{i \cdot 0}=1$

$z_{3}=e^{i\frac{\pi}{4}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$

Next, calculate the conjugates needed:

$\bar{z}_{2}=1$

$\bar{z}_{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\bar{z}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$

We need to evaluate:

$z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}+z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}+z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}$

Calculate each term separately:

$z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}) \cdot 1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$

$z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}=1 \cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}$

$z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}) \cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{(1+i)^{2}}{2}=\frac{1+2i-1}{2}=i$

Sum the evaluated terms:

$z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}+z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}+z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}})+i$

Simplify:

$=\sqrt{2}+i-\sqrt{2}i=\sqrt{2}+i(1-\sqrt{2})$

Calculate the modulus squared:

$|\sqrt{2}+i(1-\sqrt{2})|^{2}=(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(1-\sqrt{2})^{2}$

$=2+(1-2\sqrt{2}+2)=5-2\sqrt{2}$

Thus, the expression $|z_{1}\bar{z}_{2}+z_{2}\bar{z}_{3}+z_{3}\bar{z}_{1}|^{2}$ simplifies as follows:

$\alpha=5$

$\beta=-2$

Finally, compute $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ :

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=5^{2}+(-2)^{2}=25+4=29$

Therefore, the value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is 29.

questions.explanation_text: Let $z=x+iy$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow z^{2}=x^{2}-y^{2}+2ixy \\ \\ & \therefore az^{2}+bz \\ \\ & =a(x^{2}-y^{2}+2ixy)+b(x+iy) \\ \\ & =a(x^{2}-y^{2})+bx+2aixy+biy \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} Re(az^{2}+bz)=b \\ \\ \Rightarrow a(x^{2}-y^{2})+bx=a \\ \\ \Rightarrow x^{2}-y^{2}+\frac{b}{a}x=1.........(i) \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{and}bz^{2}+az \\ \\ & =b(x^{2}-y^{2}+2ixy)+a(x+iy) \\ \\ & =b(x^{2}-y^{2})+ax+2bixy+aiy \\ \\ & Re(bz^{2}+az)=b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow b(x^{2}-y^{2})+ax=b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}-y^{2}+\frac{a}{b}x=1..........(ii) \end{aligned}$ On subtracting Equation (ii) from Equation (i), we get $\begin{aligned} & \frac{b}{a}x-\frac{a}{b}x=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\frac{b}{a}-\frac{a}{b})x=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=0\text{or}\frac{b}{a}-\frac{a}{b}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow b^{2}-a^{2}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a= \pm b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a=-b(\text{since}a \ne b) \end{aligned}$ From (i), when $x=0$ , then $\begin{aligned} & 0-y^{2}=1 \Rightarrow y^{2}=-1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y \in \phi \Rightarrow z \in \phi\text{has no solution.} \end{aligned}$ When, $a=-b$ , then $x^{2}-y^{2}-x=1$ has infinitely many solutions.
questions.explanation_html:
Let $z=x+iy$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow z^{2}=x^{2}-y^{2}+2ixy \\ \\ & \therefore az^{2}+bz \\ \\ & =a(x^{2}-y^{2}+2ixy)+b(x+iy) \\ \\ & =a(x^{2}-y^{2})+bx+2aixy+biy \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} Re(az^{2}+bz)=b \\ \\ \Rightarrow a(x^{2}-y^{2})+bx=a \\ \\ \Rightarrow x^{2}-y^{2}+\frac{b}{a}x=1.........(i) \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{and}bz^{2}+az \\ \\ & =b(x^{2}-y^{2}+2ixy)+a(x+iy) \\ \\ & =b(x^{2}-y^{2})+ax+2bixy+aiy \\ \\ & Re(bz^{2}+az)=b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow b(x^{2}-y^{2})+ax=b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}-y^{2}+\frac{a}{b}x=1..........(ii) \end{aligned}$

On subtracting Equation (ii) from Equation (i), we get

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{b}{a}x-\frac{a}{b}x=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\frac{b}{a}-\frac{a}{b})x=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=0\text{or}\frac{b}{a}-\frac{a}{b}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow b^{2}-a^{2}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a= \pm b \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a=-b(\text{since}a \ne b) \end{aligned}$

From (i), when $x=0$ , then

$\begin{aligned} & 0-y^{2}=1 \Rightarrow y^{2}=-1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y \in \phi \Rightarrow z \in \phi\text{has no solution.} \end{aligned}$

When, $a=-b$ , then $x^{2}-y^{2}-x=1$ has infinitely many solutions.

questions.question_html: Let the complex number $z=x+iy$ be such that $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}$ is purely imaginary. If $x+y^{2}=0$ , then $y^{4}+y^{2}-y$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let, $z=x+iy$ So, $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}$ is purely imaginary [Given] $\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}(\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i})+(\frac{\bar{2z-3i}}{2z+i})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}+\frac{2\bar{z}+3i}{2\bar{z}-i}=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (2z-3i)(2\bar{z}-i)+(2\bar{z}+3i)(2z+i)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow {4|z|^{2}-6i\bar{z}-2iz-3}+{4|z|^{2}+6iz+2i\bar{z}-3}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8|z|^{2}-4i\bar{z}+4iz-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8(x^{2}+y^{2})-4i(x-iy)+4i(x+iy)-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8(x^{2}+y^{2})-4ix-4y+4ix-4y-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8(x^{2}+y^{2})-8y-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4(x^{2}+y^{2})-4y-3=0 \end{aligned}$ Given that, $x+y^{2}=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x=-y^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4(y^{4}+y^{2})-4y=3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y^{4}+y^{2}-y=\frac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$ Hence, required answer is $\frac{3}{4}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Let, $z=x+iy$

So, $\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}$ is purely imaginary [Given]

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}(\frac{2z-3i}{2z+i})+(\frac{\bar{2z-3i}}{2z+i})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2z-3i}{2z+i}+\frac{2\bar{z}+3i}{2\bar{z}-i}=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (2z-3i)(2\bar{z}-i)+(2\bar{z}+3i)(2z+i)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow {4|z|^{2}-6i\bar{z}-2iz-3}+{4|z|^{2}+6iz+2i\bar{z}-3}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8|z|^{2}-4i\bar{z}+4iz-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8(x^{2}+y^{2})-4i(x-iy)+4i(x+iy)-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8(x^{2}+y^{2})-4ix-4y+4ix-4y-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 8(x^{2}+y^{2})-8y-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4(x^{2}+y^{2})-4y-3=0 \end{aligned}$

Given that, $x+y^{2}=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x=-y^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4(y^{4}+y^{2})-4y=3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y^{4}+y^{2}-y=\frac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$

Hence, required answer is $\frac{3}{4}$ .

questions.question_html: Let $p,q \in ℝ$ and $(1-\sqrt{3}i)^{200}=2^{199}(p+iq),i=\sqrt{-1}$ then $p+q+q^{2}$ and $p-q+q^{2}$ are roots of the equation.
questions.explanation_text: $(1-\sqrt{3}i)^{200}$ $=[2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i)]^{200}$ $=2^{200}(cos\frac{\pi}{3}-isin\frac{\pi}{3})^{200}$ $=2^{200}(cos\frac{200\pi}{3}-isin\frac{200\pi}{3})$ $=2^{200}(cos(66\pi+\frac{2\pi}{3})-isin(66\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}))$ $=2^{200}(cos\frac{2\pi}{3}-isin\frac{2\pi}{3})$ $=2^{200}(-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i)$ $=2^{199}(-1-\sqrt{3}i)$ $=2^{199}(p+iq)$ $\therefore$ p = $-$ 1 and q = $-\sqrt{3}$ Now, $p-q+q^{2}=-1+\sqrt{3}+3=2+\sqrt{3}=\alpha$ and $p+q+q^{2}=-1-\sqrt{3}+3=2-\sqrt{3}=\beta$ $\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=4$ $\alpha\beta=(2+\sqrt{3})(2-\sqrt{3})=4-3=1$ $\therefore$ Quadratic equation is $x^{2}-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-4x+1=0$
questions.explanation_html:
$(1-\sqrt{3}i)^{200}$

$=[2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i)]^{200}$

$=2^{200}(cos\frac{\pi}{3}-isin\frac{\pi}{3})^{200}$

$=2^{200}(cos\frac{200\pi}{3}-isin\frac{200\pi}{3})$

$=2^{200}(cos(66\pi+\frac{2\pi}{3})-isin(66\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}))$

$=2^{200}(cos\frac{2\pi}{3}-isin\frac{2\pi}{3})$

$=2^{200}(-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i)$

$=2^{199}(-1-\sqrt{3}i)$

$=2^{199}(p+iq)$

$\therefore$ p = $-$ 1 and q = $-\sqrt{3}$

Now, $p-q+q^{2}=-1+\sqrt{3}+3=2+\sqrt{3}=\alpha$

and $p+q+q^{2}=-1-\sqrt{3}+3=2-\sqrt{3}=\beta$

$\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=4$

$\alpha\beta=(2+\sqrt{3})(2-\sqrt{3})=4-3=1$

$\therefore$ Quadratic equation is

$x^{2}-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-4x+1=0$

We know,

$\Rightarrow 1-\sqrt{2} \le |z| \le 1+\sqrt{2}$ ..... (1)

or

$\Rightarrow |z|^{2}-1 \le -2|z|$

$\Rightarrow |z|^{2}+2|z|-1 \le 0$

$\Rightarrow |z|^{2}+2|z|+1-2 \le 0$

$\Rightarrow (|z|+1)^{2}-2 \le 0$

$\Rightarrow -\sqrt{2} \le |z|+1 \le +\sqrt{2}$

$\Rightarrow -\sqrt{2}-1 \le |z| \le \sqrt{2}-1$ ...... (2)

From (1) and (2) we get,

Maximum value of $|z|=\sqrt{2}+1$ and minimum value of $|z|=-\sqrt{2}-1$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-2y-1=0$

$\Rightarrow x(x-1)+y(y-1)=0$

$\Rightarrow (x-\frac{1}{2})^{2}+(y-\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$



$\therefore$ $|z-(3+3i)|_{min}=|PC|-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=2\sqrt{2}$
